claim: Drosophila melanogaster is a cosmopolitan species that breeds on multiple sites, including tomatoes.
source: The common lab species, Drosophila melanogaster, is a cosmopolitan species that breeds on multiple sites, including tomatoes (Mccoy, 1962; Jaenike, 1983).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mccoy, 1962 and Jaenike, 1983

claim: When placed on a slice of fresh tomato, D. melanogaster larvae readily locate the soft middle layer of the fruit, called the locular gel, and dig into it.
source: When placed on a slice of fresh tomato, D. melanogaster larvae readily locate the soft middle layer of the fruit, called the locular gel, and dig into it (Figure 1A and A').
evidence: Supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 1A and A'

claim: The marked preference for the locular gel over the more external mescocarp layer appears to be mostly due to the soft composition of the locular gel rather than potential differences in nutritive values.
source: The marked preference for the locular gel over the more external mescocarp layer appears to be mostly due to the soft composition of the locular gel rather than potential differences in nutritive values (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Digging behavior is commonly observed in regular food vials and in behavioral assays.
source: Digging behavior is commonly observed in regular food vials and in behavioral assays (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by observational data shown in Figure 1B and C

claim: Digging takes place when the softness of low-density-agarose gels is similar to the natural habitats of Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Not surprisingly, digging takes place when the softness of low-density-agarose gels is similar to the natural habitats of Drosophila melanogaster (for stiffness measurements related to tomato pulp, see Grant et al., 2012; Li et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grant et al., 2012 and Li et al., 2012 regarding stiffness measurements

claim: Exploratory dives permit larvae to search for conditions that satisfy their metabolic and physiological needs.
source: As nutritional and pH conditions vary along the depth of a fruit, exploratory dives permit larvae to search for conditions that satisfy their metabolic and physiological needs.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the variation in nutritional and pH conditions

claim: Diving is thought to facilitate dispersal through the environment while minimizing predator encounters at the surface.
source: Diving is also thought to facilitate dispersal through the environment while minimizing predator encounters at the surface (Godoy-Herrera, 1977, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to Godoy-Herrera, 1977, 1994

claim: Cooperative digging enables populations of larvae to liquefy food sources through the effects of pre-digestive enzymes secreted in the saliva.
source: Cooperative digging enables populations of larvae to liquefy food sources through the effects of pre-digestive enzymes secreted in the saliva (Gregg et al., 1990; Chandrashekar et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gregg et al., 1990 and Chandrashekar et al., 2009

claim: Drosophila larvae are highly sensitive to humidity.
source: Like their adult counterparts (Enjin et al., 2016), Drosophila larvae are highly sensitive to humidity (Benz, 1956).
evidence: Supported by citations to Enjin et al., 2016 and Benz, 1956

claim: Dwelling into semiliquid media prevents desiccation.
source: Dwelling into semiliquid media prevents desiccation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about the relationship between humidity and desiccation

claim: Dwelling into semiliquid media enables larvae to hide from strong daylight and from predators.
source: It also enables larvae to hide from strong daylight and from predators (Hwang et al., 2007; Xiang et al., 2010; Robertson et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hwang et al., 2007; Xiang et al., 2010; Robertson et al., 2013

claim: During their exploration of the chamber, larvae dive into the hydrogel substrate for several minutes at depths larger than three times their body length.
source: During their exploration of the chamber, larvae dive into the hydrogel substrate for several minutes at depths larger than three times their body length.
evidence: Based on experimental observations in the dig-and-dive assay

claim: Larvae are air-breathing animals that cannot oxygenate underwater.
source: Since larvae are air-breathing animals that cannot oxygenate underwater (Manning and Krasnow, 1993), diving in hydrogels poses a physiological challenge.
evidence: Supported by citation to Manning and Krasnow, 1993

claim: Individuals that failed to return to the surface after a few minutes stopped moving and the majority of them drowned.
source: Individuals that failed to return to the surface after a few minutes stopped moving and the majority of them drowned.
evidence: Based on experimental observations in the dig-and-dive assay

claim: The level of oxygenation determines the propensity of larvae to dive.
source: By partially blocking the respiratory tracks of larvae, we found evidence that the level of oxygenation determines the propensity of larvae to dive.
evidence: Based on experimental manipulation of respiratory tracks

claim: Diving is regulated by a cost-benefit balance, which combines internal physiological signals with external cues.
source: This result suggests that diving is regulated by a cost-benefit balance, which combines internal physiological signals (e.g., oxygenation level and possibly hunger) with external cues (e.g., presence of food odor).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results on oxygenation and odor effects

claim: Larvae perceive and respond to liquid-borne odorant molecules.
source: Our results demonstrate that larvae perceive and respond to liquid-borne odorant molecules.
evidence: Based on experimental data showing responses to odors in liquid phase

claim: The duration of apneic dives increases upon detection of an attractive odor.
source: In line with the idea that diving relies on a cost-benefit balance adjusted by sensory signals, we found that the duration of apneic dives increases upon detection of an attractive odor.
evidence: Based on experimental data showing increased dive duration with attractive odor

claim: D. suzukii larvae are capable of digging into harder substrates than D. melanogaster.
source: Consistent with the innate preference of D. suzukii for fresh fruits, larvae of this species are capable of digging into harder substrates than D. melanogaster.
evidence: Based on experimental comparison of digging behavior in different substrate hardness

claim: D. suzukii is more resistant to hypoxia than D. melanogaster.
source: Our results indicate that D. suzukii is also more resistant to hypoxia.
evidence: Based on experimental data from spiracle blocking experiments

claim: There are species-specific differences in the modulatory effects of attractive and repulsive odors on the dig-and-dive behavior of D. melanogaster and D. suzukii.
source: Finally, we report the existence of species-specific differences in the modulatory effects of attractive and repulsive odors on the dig-and-dive behavior of D. melanogaster and D. suzukii.
evidence: Based on experimental comparison of odor responses between species

claim: At the surface, larvae tended to be inactive.
source: At the surface, larvae tended to be inactive.
evidence: Based on observational data from the dig-and-dive assay

claim: While immersed in the agarose gel, larvae oriented head down and kept their spiracles in contact with the air at the gel's interface.
source: While immersed in the agarose gel, larvae demonstrated two different types of behavior: right under the surface, they oriented head down and kept their spiracles in contact with the air at the gel's interface (Figure 2B).
evidence: Based on observational data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Larval digging is commonly observed in transparent food vials in the lab.
source: Larval digging is commonly observed in transparent food vials in the lab (Figure 1B) (Sokolowski, 1982).
evidence: Supported by observational data in Figure 1B and citation to Sokolowski, 1982

claim: Digging permits larvae to feed and breathe while staying hidden from predators at the surface.
source: Digging permits larvae to feed and breathe while staying hidden from predators at the surface.
evidence: Based on inference from the snorkeling behavior and ecological context

claim: Individual dives lasted up to a couple of hundred seconds during which the larva remained active until it returned to the surface.
source: Individual dives lasted up to a couple of hundred seconds during which the larva remained active until it returned to the surface.
evidence: Based on experimental measurements from the dig-and-dive assay

claim: The mean of the PDF of larval centroid depth was located 2.7 mm below the surface of the gel.
source: The mean of the PDF was located 2.7 mm below the surface of the gel.
evidence: Based on quantitative analysis of position data

claim: Larvae appeared to be actively feeding through the contraction of their mouth hook during digging.
source: As larvae appeared to be actively feeding through the contraction of their mouth hook (Sokolowski, 1982; Green et al., 1983; Schoofs et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2013), digging can be associated with the exploitation of the medium (Cohen et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by observational data and citations to Sokolowski, 1982; Green et al., 1983; Schoofs et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2013; Cohen et al., 2007

claim: Digging can be associated with the exploitation of the medium.
source: As larvae appeared to be actively feeding through the contraction of their mouth hook (Sokolowski, 1982; Green et al., 1983; Schoofs et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2013), digging can be associated with the exploitation of the medium (Cohen et al., 2007).
evidence: Based on inference from feeding behavior and citation to Cohen et al., 2007

claim: During diving, oxygenation at the surface was interrupted and larvae became hypoxic.
source: The bottom part of the PDF (Z ≤ Zdiving) corresponded to diving behavior during which oxygenation at the surface was interrupted and larvae became hypoxic (Morton, 2011).
evidence: Based on inference from the diving behavior and citation to Morton, 2011

claim: Diving can be associated with the exploration of the medium.
source: Diving can be associated with the exploration of the medium.
evidence: Based on inference from the behavioral context

claim: The stiffness of an agarose gel is proportional to the percentage of agarose mixed with water.
source: We took advantage of the fact that the stiffness of an agarose gel is proportional to the percentage of agarose mixed with water (Grant et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grant et al., 2012

claim: In low-percentage agarose gels (0.05% w/v), surfacing was the dominant behavioral mode in D. melanogaster.
source: In low-percentage agarose gels (0.05% w/v), surfacing was the dominant behavioral mode in D. melanogaster (Figure 3A).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Nearly no diving was observed in 0.05% agarose gels.
source: Nearly no diving was observed in 0.05% agarose gels (Figure 3A), suggesting that motion through peristalsis is inefficient in soft hydrogels (Video 1).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Video 1

claim: Motion through peristalsis is inefficient in soft hydrogels.
source: Nearly no diving was observed in 0.05% agarose gels (Figure 3A), suggesting that motion through peristalsis is inefficient in soft hydrogels (Video 1).
evidence: Based on inference from the lack of diving in soft gels

claim: D. melanogaster larvae actively avoided soft substrates after having experienced their textures.
source: The peak of the PDF corresponding to 0.05% agarose gels coincided with the top of the air chamber, indicating that D. melanogaster larvae actively avoided soft substrates after having experienced their textures (Video 1).
evidence: Based on analysis of position distribution data and Video 1

claim: Individuals that failed to return to the surface stopped moving after a few minutes.
source: Individuals that failed to return to the surface stopped moving after a few minutes.
evidence: Based on observational data from the dig-and-dive assay

claim: Inactive larvae were found to have drowned.
source: Given that inactive larvae were found to have drowned (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), immersed animals that stopped being active were not included in the analysis.
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: In hard media of 2% agarose, larvae rested at the surface of the gel during ~80% of the trial with short periods of digging.
source: In the other extreme condition of hardness, larvae were tested in hard media of 2% agarose (Video 2). In this condition, larvae rested at the surface of the gel during ~80% of the trial with short periods of digging (Figure 3A).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Video 2

claim: For densities equal to or higher than 3% agarose, D. melanogaster larvae could neither dig nor dive into the substrate.
source: For densities equal to or higher than 3% agarose, D. melanogaster larvae could neither dig nor dive into the substrate (Louis et al., 2008; Apostolopoulou et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Louis et al., 2008 and Apostolopoulou et al., 2014

claim: The largest percentage of time spent in dive mode was observed in gels of intermediate hardness (0.2% agarose).
source: The largest percentage of time spent in dive mode was observed in gels of intermediate hardness (0.2% agarose).
evidence: Based on experimental data comparing different agarose concentrations

claim: For media with an agarose percentage higher than 0.2%, the median duration of individual dives decreased with the hardness of the gel.
source: For media with an agarose percentage higher than 0.2%, the median duration of individual dives decreased with the hardness of the gel, and so did the maximum dive depth (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: The maximum dive depth decreased with the hardness of the gel for media with an agarose percentage higher than 0.2%.
source: For media with an agarose percentage higher than 0.2%, the median duration of individual dives decreased with the hardness of the gel, and so did the maximum dive depth (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: D. melanogaster larvae spent most of their time at the surface when the environment was either too soft or too hard.
source: In summary, we found that D. melanogaster larvae spent most of their time at the surface when the environment was either too soft or too hard.
evidence: Based on synthesis of experimental data across different substrate hardness conditions

claim: For media with intermediate textures, diving tended to be suppressed as the hardness of the substrate increased.
source: For media with intermediate textures, the balance between digging and diving was influenced by the stiffness of the gel: diving tended to be suppressed as the hardness of the substrate increased (Figure 3).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: The difficulty of D. melanogaster larvae to dig into hard substrates probably explains their preference for the internal soft layers of tomato slices.
source: The difficulty of D. melanogaster larvae to dig into hard substrates probably explains their preference for the internal soft layers of tomato slices (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data on substrate hardness and tomato preference

claim: The respiration system of the Drosophila larva is composed of two parallel tracheae that terminate in anterior and posterior spiracles enabling gas exchange with the external environment.
source: The respiration system of the Drosophila larva is composed of two parallel tracheae that terminate in anterior and posterior spiracles enabling gas exchange with the external environment (Figure 4A) (Manning and Krasnow, 1993).
evidence: Supported by Figure 4A and citation to Manning and Krasnow, 1993

claim: In the tracheae of the larva, longitudinal transport of oxygen takes place by means of passive diffusion.
source: In the tracheae of the larva, longitudinal transport of oxygen takes place by means of passive diffusion (Krogh, 1920).
evidence: Supported by citation to Krogh, 1920

claim: Upon submersion into liquid, the extremities of the anterior and the posterior spiracles are closed by hydrophobic hairs.
source: Upon submersion into liquid, the extremities of the anterior and the posterior spiracles are closed by hydrophobic hairs (Manning and Krasnow, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to Manning and Krasnow, 1993

claim: The two posterior spiracles can be viewed as 'snorkeling' devices that enable larvae to stay oxygenated while digging into the medium.
source: As larvae feed head-down with their posterior end in contact with the surface (Figure 2B, right panel), the two posterior spiracles can be viewed as 'snorkeling' devices that enable larvae to stay oxygenated while digging into the medium.
evidence: Based on inference from the anatomical arrangement and behavioral observations

claim: During digging and diving, the anterior spiracles are immersed and retracted inside the head to prevent the flow of external liquid into the tracheae.
source: During digging and diving, the anterior spiracles are immersed and retracted inside the head (Manning and Krasnow, 1993) to prevent the flow of external liquid into the tracheae.
evidence: Supported by citation to Manning and Krasnow, 1993 and inference about function

claim: During digging, gas exchange is still achieved through the posterior spiracles, which allows larvae to stay oxygenated without having to fully surface during the entire duration of an experiment.
source: During digging, gas exchange is still achieved through the posterior spiracles, which allows larvae to stay oxygenated through their posterior spiracles without having to fully surface during the entire duration of an experiment.
evidence: Based on inference from the snorkeling behavior and respiratory anatomy

claim: Diving is limited by the lack of oxygenation following the loss of contact of the spiracles with the surface.
source: By contrast, diving is limited by the lack of oxygenation following the loss of contact of the spiracles with the surface.
evidence: Based on inference from the respiratory physiology

claim: When larvae are unable to return to the surface to re-oxygenate, movements stop.
source: When larvae are unable to return to the surface to re-oxygenate, movements stop.
evidence: Based on observational data from the dig-and-dive assay

claim: The lack of movement coincides with drowning.
source: In Figure 3—figure supplement 1, we established that the lack of movement coincides with drowning.
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: D. melanogaster larvae with blocked posterior spiracles were unharmed and capable of breathing through their anterior spiracles.
source: D. melanogaster larvae with blocked posterior spiracles were unharmed and capable of breathing through their anterior spiracles.
evidence: Based on experimental observation of larvae with blocked spiracles

claim: The locomotor activity (average speed) of larvae with blocked posterior spiracles was not strongly impaired during motion on two-dimensional agarose surfaces.
source: We controlled that their locomotor activity (average speed) was not strongly impaired during motion on two-dimensional (2D) agarose surfaces (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: There were no differences in locomotor patterns (body postures) between larvae with intact and blocked posterior spiracles.
source: In addition, we verified the absence of differences in locomotor patterns (body postures) between larvae with intact and blocked posterior spiracles (Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: Based on video analysis shown in Videos 3 and 4

claim: Larvae with blocked posterior spiracles displayed dramatic differences in the organization of their exploratory behavior in the dig-and-dive assay.
source: In spite of their normal locomotor behavior, larvae with blocked posterior spiracles displayed dramatic differences in the organization of their exploratory behavior in the dig-and-dive assay.
evidence: Based on experimental comparison of behavior with and without spiracle block

claim: Deficient respiration produced a strong suppression of digging and diving.
source: Deficient respiration produced a strong suppression of digging and diving (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 4B and C

claim: Upon block of the posterior spiracles, the percentage of time spent digging and diving was significantly decreased whereas the time spent surfacing increased.
source: Upon block of the posterior spiracles, the percentage of time spent digging and diving was significantly decreased whereas the time spent surfacing increased (Figure 4D).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Exploratory dives induce hypoxic stress that forces larvae to stay at the surface.
source: Based on these results, we speculate that exploratory dives induce hypoxic stress that forces larvae to stay at the surface.
evidence: Based on speculation from the spiracle blocking experiments

claim: Diving can be viewed as a form of risk-taking behavior, which is part of the larval foraging strategy.
source: In line with the active avoidance of very soft substrates that pose a risk of drowning during dives (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), diving can be viewed as a form of risk-taking behavior, which is part of the larval foraging strategy.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data on substrate avoidance and drowning risk

claim: Odorant molecules detected in gaseous phase direct orientation behavior in larvae crawling on 2D agarose surfaces.
source: Odorant molecules detected in gaseous phase direct orientation behavior in larvae crawling on 2D agarose surfaces (Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2012

claim: Ethyl acetate was used due to its high solubility in water (82.2 g/L at 22°C) and the strength of the chemotactic behavior it elicits in gaseous phase.
source: Ethyl acetate (EtA, 40 mM of aqueous solution) was used due to its high solubility in water (82.2 g/L at 22°C) and the strength of the chemotactic behavior it elicits in gaseous phase (Kreher et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kreher et al., 2008 and knowledge about ethyl acetate properties

claim: D. melanogaster larvae were tested in 0.4% agarose gels that included a stable odor gradient pointing from the surface down to the bottom of the assay.
source: D. melanogaster larvae were tested in 0.4% agarose gels that included a stable odor gradient pointing from the surface down to the bottom of the assay (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on experimental setup shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: In the absence of odor, D. melanogaster larvae displayed infrequent dives that were short-lived and shallow.
source: In the absence of odor, D. melanogaster larvae displayed infrequent dives that were short-lived and shallow (Figure 5A and C, and Video 5).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 5A and C, and Video 5

claim: The presence of the odor induced a significant prolongation of individual dives together with an increase in dive frequency and dive depth.
source: By contrast, the presence of the odor induced a significant prolongation of individual dives together with an increase in dive frequency and dive depth (Figure 5B and C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, and Video 6).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, and Video 6

claim: The percentage of time spent in diving mode increased in presence of the odor.
source: As a result, the percentage of time spent in diving mode increased in presence of the odor (Figure 5D).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: The increase in dive time was coupled to a marginal increase in the number of dives.
source: The increase in dive time was coupled to a marginal increase in the number of dives (average number of dives: 4.1 ± 3.2 in absence of odor and 5.3 ± 2.5 in presence of odor).
evidence: Based on quantitative analysis of dive frequency

claim: The presence of the odor promoted diving shortly after the beginning of the trial.
source: While larvae did not dive into the medium directly upon their introduction in a chamber devoid of odor, the presence of the odor promoted diving shortly after the beginning of the trial (Figure 5C, right panel).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Olfactory stimulation had a synchronizing effect on the behavior of larvae across trials.
source: Therefore, olfactory stimulation had a synchronizing effect on the behavior of larvae across trials.
evidence: Based on inference from the timing of dives across trials

claim: The increase in the probability of diving was sustained for several minutes compared to the condition without odor.
source: This increase in the probability of diving was sustained for several minutes compared to the condition without odor (Figure 5E).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Larvae dived deeper and longer in the presence of the odor.
source: These two functions showed that larvae dived deeper and longer in the presence of the odor.
evidence: Based on analysis of cumulative distribution functions of dive parameters

claim: The durations of individual dives increased with the maximum dive depth.
source: The durations of individual dives increased with the maximum dive depth.
evidence: Based on correlation analysis of dive parameters

claim: The depths of individual dives increased in presence of the odor.
source: Moreover, the depths of individual dives increased in presence of the odor (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C

claim: D. melanogaster larvae spent more time searching for the odor source at the bottom of the chamber.
source: This result suggests that D. melanogaster larvae spent more time searching for the odor source at the bottom of the chamber.
evidence: Based on inference from the increased dive depth and duration with odor

claim: The presence of the odor led to a non-significant increase in dive frequency.
source: On the other hand, the presence of the odor led to a non-significant increase in dive frequency while the dive speed remained unchanged (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D and E

claim: The dive speed remained unchanged in presence of the odor.
source: On the other hand, the presence of the odor led to a non-significant increase in dive frequency while the dive speed remained unchanged (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D and E

claim: There is no correlation between the duration of a dive and the duration of surfacing that followed diving.
source: We observed no correlation between the duration of a dive and the duration of surfacing that followed diving (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2F

claim: Most dives did not reach their aerobic limit.
source: This result argues that most dives did not reach their aerobic limit (Kooyman et al., 1980; Boyd, 1997).
evidence: Based on inference from the lack of correlation between dive and surfacing duration, supported by citations to Kooyman et al., 1980 and Boyd, 1997

claim: Larvae with impaired olfactory function did not respond to the presence of the liquid-borne odor.
source: Larvae with impaired olfactory function did not respond to the presence of the liquid-borne odor (Figure 5D).
evidence: Based on experimental data with anosmic larvae shown in Figure 5D

claim: The behavioral response elicited by liquid-borne odors is not predominantly mediated by the gustatory system.
source: This established that the behavioral response elicited by liquid-borne odors is not predominantly mediated by the gustatory system.
evidence: Based on inference from the lack of response in anosmic larvae

claim: Larvae can make use of the detection of odors in liquid phase to direct explorative dives toward a potential food source.
source: Taken together, the previous results indicate that larvae can make use of the detection of odors in liquid phase to direct explorative dives toward a potential food source.
evidence: Based on synthesis of experimental results on liquid-borne odor detection

claim: Diving is nearly fully impaired when larvae detect the presence of natural food (yeast) mixed with the substrate.
source: In agreement with this idea, diving is nearly fully impaired when larvae detect the presence of natural food (yeast) mixed with the substrate (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3

claim: The addition of sugar (fructose) alone to the substrate had the same blocking effect on diving as yeast.
source: The addition of sugar (fructose) alone to the substrate was found to have the same blocking effect on diving (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4

claim: Sugar promoted feeding behavior through repeated mouth hook contractions during digging but not during diving.
source: Moreover, sugar promoted feeding behavior through repeated mouth hook contractions during digging but not during diving (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5

claim: The basal rate of mouth hook contraction observed during diving is part of the locomotor program that permits larvae to move in the agarose substrate.
source: The basal rate of mouth hook contraction observed during diving is part of the locomotor program that permits larvae to move in the agarose substrate.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation of mouth hook contractions during diving

claim: Diving can be viewed as an exploratory food-search behavior that can be driven by olfactory cues but that is largely uncoupled from active feeding.
source: In conclusion, diving can be viewed as an exploratory food-search behavior that can be driven by olfactory cues but that is largely uncoupled from active feeding.
evidence: Based on synthesis of experimental results on odor effects and feeding behavior

claim: Drosophila species experience a wide variety of food resources whose properties differ in stiffness and nutrient composition.
source: In nature, Drosophila species experience a wide variety of food resources whose properties differ in stiffness and nutrient composition (Hansson and Stensmyr, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hansson and Stensmyr, 2011

claim: Digging and diving behaviors between different species are expected to partially reflect an adaption to differences in food resources and ecological niches.
source: Digging and diving behaviors between different species are expected to partially reflect an adaption to differences in food resources and ecological niches.
evidence: Based on inference from ecological principles

claim: D. suzukii preferentially targets fresh (hard) fruits over (soft) rotten fruits for egg laying.
source: Unlike D. melanogaster, D. suzukii preferentially targets fresh (hard) fruits over (soft) rotten fruits for egg laying (Karageorgi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Karageorgi et al., 2017

claim: In soft media (0.05%) in which peristaltic locomotion was mostly impaired in D. melanogaster, D. suzukii larvae did not refrain from diving.
source: In soft media (0.05%) in which peristaltic locomotion was mostly impaired in D. melanogaster (Figure 3A and Video 1), D. suzukii larvae did not refrain from diving (Figure 6A and Video 7).
evidence: Based on experimental comparison shown in Figure 6A and Video 7

claim: In media with intermediate hardness (0.4%), the fraction of time spent diving was significantly larger for D. suzukii than for D. melanogaster.
source: In media with intermediate hardness (0.4%), the fraction of time spent diving was significantly larger for D. suzukii than for D. melanogaster (Figure 6D).
evidence: Based on experimental comparison shown in Figure 6D

claim: The average number of dives per trial was lower for D. suzukii than for D. melanogaster.
source: As observed in the ethogram of Figure 6B, the average number of dives per trial was lower for D. suzukii than for D. melanogaster (1.9 ± 1.5 and 4.1 ± 3.2, respectively).
evidence: Based on quantitative analysis of ethogram data in Figure 6B

claim: The increase of the fraction of time spent in dive mode resulted from a tenfold increase in the duration of individual dives for D. suzukii.
source: The increase of the fraction of time spent in dive mode resulted from a tenfold increase in the duration of individual dives (Figure 6C), reflecting the higher tolerance of D. suzukii larvae to hypoxia.
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 6C

claim: The tenfold increase in dive duration reflects the higher tolerance of D. suzukii larvae to hypoxia.
source: The increase of the fraction of time spent in dive mode resulted from a tenfold increase in the duration of individual dives (Figure 6C), reflecting the higher tolerance of D. suzukii larvae to hypoxia.
evidence: Based on inference from the increased dive duration

claim: The enhanced robustness of D. suzukii to hypoxic stress induced by a block of its posterior spiracles corroborates the hypothesis of higher tolerance to hypoxia.
source: This hypothesis was corroborated by the enhanced robustness of D. suzukii to hypoxic stress induced by a block of its posterior spiracles (Figure 6D).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 6D

claim: D. suzukii dived deeper than D. melanogaster.
source: Overall, D. suzukii dived deeper than D. melanogaster (black traces, Figure 8—figure supplement 1) and D. suzukii initiated diving earlier during the trial (Figure 6B to be compared with Figure 5C, left panel).
evidence: Based on experimental comparison shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1

claim: D. suzukii initiated diving earlier during the trial than D. melanogaster.
source: Overall, D. suzukii dived deeper than D. melanogaster (black traces, Figure 8—figure supplement 1) and D. suzukii initiated diving earlier during the trial (Figure 6B to be compared with Figure 5C, left panel).
evidence: Based on experimental comparison of ethograms in Figure 6B and Figure 5C

claim: Blocking the spiracles of D. suzukii reduced the average number of dives per trial.
source: Although blocking the spiracles of D. suzukii reduced the average number of dives per trial (1.9 ± 1.5 versus 1.0 ± 0.9, respectively), it did not severely decrease the percentage of time spent in dive mode (Figure 6D).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 6D

claim: Blocking the spiracles of D. suzukii did not severely decrease the percentage of time spent in dive mode.
source: Although blocking the spiracles of D. suzukii reduced the average number of dives per trial (1.9 ± 1.5 versus 1.0 ± 0.9, respectively), it did not severely decrease the percentage of time spent in dive mode (Figure 6D).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 6D

claim: D. suzukii larvae showed a fourfold increase in cumulated digging time compared to D. melanogaster in hard media (2%).
source: In hard media (2%), D. suzukii larvae showed a fourfold increase in cumulated digging time compared to D. melanogaster, strengthening the idea that the ability of D. suzukii to grow on fresh fruits is coupled with an adaptation to dig and dive into hard substrates (Video 8 and Figure 6A for D. suzukii to be compared to Figure 3A for D. melanogaster).
evidence: Based on experimental comparison shown in Video 8, Figure 6A and Figure 3A

claim: The ability of D. suzukii to grow on fresh fruits is coupled with an adaptation to dig and dive into hard substrates.
source: In hard media (2%), D. suzukii larvae showed a fourfold increase in cumulated digging time compared to D. melanogaster, strengthening the idea that the ability of D. suzukii to grow on fresh fruits is coupled with an adaptation to dig and dive into hard substrates (Video 8 and Figure 6A for D. suzukii to be compared to Figure 3A for D. melanogaster).
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data on digging in hard substrates

claim: D. suzukii larvae displayed a preference for soft substrates when given a choice.
source: When given a choice, D. suzukii larvae nonetheless displayed a preference for soft substrates (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) — a phenomenon also observed for feeding behavior at the adult stage (Karageorgi et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and citation to Karageorgi et al., 2017

claim: Ethyl acetate is attractive to D. suzukii in gaseous phase.
source: First, we established the attractiveness of ethyl acetate to D. suzukii in a standard chemotaxis assay in which the odor was delivered in gaseous phase (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: Ethyl acetate led to a significant reduction in total dive time in D. suzukii when presented in the dig-and-dive assay.
source: When presented in the dig-and-dive assay, ethyl acetate led to a significant reduction in total dive time in D. suzukii (Figure 7B) with no dramatic decrease in the duration of individual dives (median times of 1.1 and 0.8 min for the no-odor and the odor conditions, respectively; Wilcoxon rank-sum test p=0.24).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 7B

claim: There was no dramatic decrease in the duration of individual dives in D. suzukii with ethyl acetate.
source: When presented in the dig-and-dive assay, ethyl acetate led to a significant reduction in total dive time in D. suzukii (Figure 7B) with no dramatic decrease in the duration of individual dives (median times of 1.1 and 0.8 min for the no-odor and the odor conditions, respectively; Wilcoxon rank-sum test p=0.24).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of dive duration data

claim: There was no obvious reduction in the average number of dives with and without odor in D. suzukii.
source: While a decrease in the number of dives is expected for aversive responses, we found no obvious reduction in the average number of dives with and without odor (2.0 ± 1.2 and 1.9 ± 1.5, respectively).
evidence: Based on quantitative analysis of dive frequency

claim: The lack of reduction in dive number is consistent with the observation that ethyl acetate is an odor attractive to D. suzukii in gaseous phase.
source: This latter result is consistent with the observation that ethyl acetate is an odor attractive to D. suzukii in gaseous phase (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on inference from the dive frequency data and gaseous phase attraction data

claim: Even in the absence of odor, D. suzukii frequently reached the bottom of the chamber.
source: We then considered the depth to which each species dived. Even in the absence of odor, D. suzukii frequently reached the bottom of the chamber.
evidence: Based on analysis of dive depth data

claim: D. melanogaster performed shallower dives than D. suzukii in the absence of odor.
source: By contrast, D. melanogaster performed shallower dives (the maximum dive depth for D. suzukii and D. melanogaster is 7.1 ± 3.4 mm and 5.2 ± 1.6 mm, respectively).
evidence: Based on quantitative comparison of dive depth data

claim: In presence of ethyl acetate, D. melanogaster dived as deep as D. suzukii.
source: In presence of ethyl acetate, D. melanogaster dived as deep as D. suzukii (6.6 ± 2.7 mm and 6.6 ± 3.0 mm, respectively).
evidence: Based on quantitative comparison of dive depth data with odor

claim: Ethyl acetate is unlikely to act as a repellent in D. suzukii.
source: Since the odor affected neither the time spent at the surface (Figure 7B) nor the average dive depth, we concluded that ethyl acetate is unlikely to act as a repellent in D. suzukii.
evidence: Based on inference from the lack of effect on surfacing time and dive depth

claim: Ethyl acetate synchronized diving at the beginning of the trial in D. suzukii.
source: Although the odor synchronized diving at the beginning of the trial (Figure 7C), the increase in dive probability was only transient compared to the sustained stimulation of diving in D. melanogaster (Figure 5E).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 7C

claim: The increase in dive probability was only transient in D. suzukii compared to the sustained stimulation of diving in D. melanogaster.
source: Although the odor synchronized diving at the beginning of the trial (Figure 7C), the increase in dive probability was only transient compared to the sustained stimulation of diving in D. melanogaster (Figure 5E).
evidence: Based on comparison of temporal dynamics shown in Figure 7C and Figure 5E

claim: D. suzukii undergo a transient attractive response to the food-odor ethyl acetate in the dig-and-dive assay.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that D. suzukii undergo a transient attractive response to the food-odor ethyl acetate in the dig-and-dive assay.
evidence: Based on synthesis of experimental results on ethyl acetate effects in D. suzukii

claim: The transient nature of the response in D. suzukii contrasts with the persistent attraction the odor elicited in D. melanogaster.
source: The transient nature of the response in D. suzukii contrasts with the persistent attraction the odor elicited in D. melanogaster.
evidence: Based on comparison of temporal dynamics between species

claim: Geosmin is an earthy volatile chemical produced by fungi and bacteria.
source: Finally, we examined the modulatory effect of a repulsive odor, geosmin — an earthy volatile chemical produced by fungi and bacteria.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about geosmin

claim: Geosmin has been shown to elicit avoidance responses in adult flies of D. melanogaster and D. suzukii.
source: Geosmin has been shown to elicit avoidance responses in adult flies of D. melanogaster and D. suzukii (Stensmyr et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stensmyr et al., 2012

claim: For both D. melanogaster and D. suzukii, detection of geosmin affected the dynamics of the dig-and-dive behavior.
source: For both D. melanogaster and D. suzukii, detection of geosmin affected the dynamics of the dig-and-dive behavior.
evidence: Based on experimental data comparing behavior with and without geosmin

claim: Several aspects of the behavioral modulation by geosmin were species-specific.
source: However, several aspects of the behavioral modulation were species-specific.
evidence: Based on comparison of geosmin effects between species

claim: For D. melanogaster, geosmin did not induce a significant change in the fraction of time spent diving, but it significantly increased surfacing time.
source: For D. melanogaster, geosmin did not induce a significant change in the fraction of time spent diving, but it significantly increased surfacing time — a trend characteristic of aversion (Figure 8B and C).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 8B and C

claim: The increase in surfacing time by geosmin is a trend characteristic of aversion.
source: For D. melanogaster, geosmin did not induce a significant change in the fraction of time spent diving, but it significantly increased surfacing time — a trend characteristic of aversion (Figure 8B and C).
evidence: Based on inference from the behavioral pattern

claim: Surfacing larvae avoided contact with the gel when exposed to geosmin, corroborating the idea that geosmin acted as a repellent in D. melanogaster.
source: While surfacing larvae avoided contact with the gel, corroborating the idea that geosmin acted as a repellent in D. melanogaster (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A

claim: Geosmin had a synchronizing effect on the first dive at the beginning of the trial in D. melanogaster.
source: It was nonetheless observed that geosmin had a synchronizing effect on the first dive at the beginning of the trial (Figure 8C).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 8C

claim: D. melanogaster showed a transient attractive response at the beginning of the trial that turned into prolonged aversion when exposed to geosmin.
source: Thus, D. melanogaster showed a transient attractive response at the beginning of the trial that turned into prolonged aversion.
evidence: Based on inference from the temporal dynamics of the behavioral response

claim: For D. suzukii, geosmin produced a significant decrease in the fraction of time spent diving.
source: For D. suzukii, geosmin produced a significant decrease in the fraction of time spent diving (Figure 8E) coupled with a significant increase in surfacing time.
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 8E

claim: For D. suzukii, geosmin produced a significant increase in surfacing time.
source: For D. suzukii, geosmin produced a significant decrease in the fraction of time spent diving (Figure 8E) coupled with a significant increase in surfacing time.
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 8E

claim: Geosmin suppressed diving shortly after the beginning of the trial in D. suzukii.
source: Geosmin suppressed diving shortly after the beginning of the trial (left panel of Figure 8F).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 8F

claim: Geosmin decreased the probability of diving deeper and increased the probability of staying above the surface of the gel in D. suzukii.
source: It also decreased the probability of diving deeper and increased the probability of staying above the surface of the gel (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B

claim: The ethogram of D. suzukii illustrates the emergence of a fourth behavioral mode: escaping out of the arena through the air channels.
source: The ethogram of D. suzukii illustrates the emergence of a fourth behavioral mode: escaping out of the arena through the air channels (light gray traces in Figure 8D).
evidence: Based on observational data shown in Figure 8D

claim: Escaping must be a behavior that requires substantial energy considering the difference between the diameter of the air channels and the diameter of the larval body.
source: Considering the difference between the diameter of the air channels (~0.2 mm) through which larvae attempted to escape and the diameter of the larval body (~1 mm), escaping must be a behavior that requires substantial energy.
evidence: Based on inference from the physical constraints of escaping

claim: Upon stimulation with geosmin, a quarter of the D. suzukii larvae escaped the assay while none did so in absence of the chemical.
source: Upon stimulation with geosmin, a quarter of the larvae escaped the assay while none did so in absence of the chemical.
evidence: Based on quantitative analysis of escape behavior

claim: Geosmin acts as a repellent in the D. melanogaster and D. suzukii species: it promotes exit and escape from the substrate.
source: Based on these observations, we conclude that geosmin acts as a repellent in the D. melanogaster and D. suzukii species: it promotes exit and escape from the substrate.
evidence: Based on synthesis of experimental results on geosmin effects

claim: Similar escape responses were observed for D. suzukii exposed to the common insect repellent DEET.
source: As shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2, similar escape responses were observed for D. suzukii exposed to the common insect repellent DEET (N,N-Diethyl-meta-toluamide, Brown and Hebert, 1997; Ditzen et al., 2008; Katz et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2 and citations to Brown and Hebert, 1997; Ditzen et al., 2008; Katz et al., 2008

claim: The use of non-toxic chemicals could refrain D. suzukii larvae from digging and diving, which in turn would slow down feeding and development and increase exposure to parasitoid wasps at the surface of fruits.
source: Together, these observations highlight the potential of pest control strategies in which the use of non-toxic chemicals could refrain D. suzukii larvae from digging and diving, which in turn would slow down feeding and development and increase exposure to parasitoid wasps at the surface of fruits (Cini et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on speculation about pest control applications and citation to Cini et al., 2012

claim: Such strategies could complement existing efforts to lure adult flies into traps filled with attractive volatile chemicals.
source: Such strategies could complement existing efforts to lure adult flies into traps filled with attractive volatile chemicals (Walsh et al., 2011; Abraham et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on speculation about pest control applications and citations to Walsh et al., 2011 and Abraham et al., 2015

claim: The dig-and-dive assay appears well suited to identify and to characterize the effects of pheromones involved in aggregation behavior.
source: Furthermore, the dig-and-dive assay appears well suited to identify and to characterize the effects of pheromones involved in aggregation behavior (Gregg et al., 1990; Mast et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on speculation about future applications and citations to Gregg et al., 1990 and Mast et al., 2014

claim: Knowledge about pheromones might guide future efforts to devise methods to interfere with the ability of larvae to aggregate and to destroy crops by feeding through their dig-and-dive behavior.
source: This knowledge might guide future efforts to devise methods to interfere with the ability of larvae to aggregate and to destroy crops by feeding through their dig-and-dive behavior.
evidence: Based on speculation about future pest control applications

claim: The alternation between sequences of apneic dives and surfacing is reminiscent of food search behaviors in sea mammals.
source: The alternation between sequences of apneic dives and surfacing is reminiscent of food search behaviors in sea mammals.
evidence: Based on inference from comparison with sea mammal behavior

claim: Whales, seals and turtles seek food during dives interspaced with resting phases at the surface.
source: Whales, seals and turtles seek food during dives interspaced with resting phases at the surface (Boyd, 1997; Tyack et al., 2006; Houghton et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boyd, 1997; Tyack et al., 2006; Houghton et al., 2008

claim: The lack of correlation between the duration of single dives and the subsequent resting phase suggests that most sea mammals perform aerobic dives.
source: The lack of correlation between the duration of single dives and the subsequent resting phase suggests that most sea mammals perform aerobic dives (Boyd, 1997; Hooker and Baird, 1999).
evidence: Based on inference from correlation analysis and citations to Boyd, 1997 and Hooker and Baird, 1999

claim: The same conclusion about aerobic dives can be drawn for the D. melanogaster larva.
source: The same conclusion can be drawn for the D. melanogaster larva (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on inference from correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: The importance of olfactory cues has been established in the food-search behavior of terrestrial insects, reptiles and mammals.
source: The importance of olfactory cues has been established in the food-search behavior of terrestrial insects, reptiles and mammals (Fraenkel and Gunn, 1961) as well as birds, crustaceans and fishes (Guilford et al., 1998; DeBose and Nevitt, 2008; Nevitt et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fraenkel and Gunn, 1961; Guilford et al., 1998; DeBose and Nevitt, 2008; Nevitt et al., 2008

claim: Olfaction is key to the survival of Drosophila larvae: attractive odors guide larvae towards food sources.
source: Olfaction is key to the survival of Drosophila larvae: attractive odors guide larvae towards food sources (Asahina et al., 2008; Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Asahina et al., 2008 and Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2012

claim: Feeding in larvae is facilitated by the aggregation of groups of larvae that expel digestive enzymes in their saliva — a process called social digestion.
source: Feeding in larvae is also facilitated by the aggregation of groups of larvae that expel digestive enzymes in their saliva — a process called social digestion (Gregg et al., 1990; Sakaguchi and Suzuki, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gregg et al., 1990 and Sakaguchi and Suzuki, 2013

claim: Spatial aggregation of larvae relies on the detection of pheromones.
source: Spatial aggregation of larvae relies on the detection of pheromones (Mast et al., 2014; Del Pino et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mast et al., 2014 and Del Pino et al., 2015

claim: In contrast with the sustained attraction elicited by ethyl acetate in gaseous phase, this odor did not promote sustained diving in D. suzukii after a first dive.
source: In contrast with the sustained attraction elicited by ethyl acetate in gaseous phase (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), this odor did not promote sustained diving in D. suzukii after a first dive (Figure 7C).
evidence: Based on comparison of temporal dynamics shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7C

claim: D. suzukii limits its exploratory dives after having experienced a first search that did not result in the successful discovery of food.
source: Considering the fact that D. suzukii dives longer (Figure 6C) but less frequently than D. melanogaster (1.9 ± 1.4 versus 4.1 ± 3.1 in absence of odor), we speculate that D. suzukii limits its exploratory dives after having experienced a first search that did not result in the successful discovery of food.
evidence: Based on speculation from the dive frequency and duration data

claim: D. melanogaster does not appear to be deterred by unsuccessful dives.
source: By contrast, D. melanogaster does not appear to be deterred by unsuccessful dives (Figure 5C and D, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on inference from the dive frequency data shown in Figure 5C and D, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: D. melanogaster and D. suzukii appear to have evolved different ways to weigh the factors that control the balance between surfacing, digging (exploitation) and exploratory dives.
source: Overall, D. melanogaster and D. suzukii appear to have evolved different ways to weigh the factors that control the balance between surfacing, digging (exploitation) and exploratory dives.
evidence: Based on synthesis of experimental results comparing the two species

claim: Effective food search necessitates combining chemosensory cues with contextual information related to the physiological state and the history of the animal in both species.
source: In both species, effective food search necessitates combining chemosensory cues with contextual information related to the physiological state and the history of the animal.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental results on sensory and physiological modulation

claim: Recent work has highlighted the crucial role played by olfaction and nutrient homeostasis in the control of food-search behavior in adult flies.
source: Although the neural circuitry that computes the cost-benefit balance remains to be identified, recent work has highlighted the crucial role played by olfaction and nutrient homeostasis in the control of food-search behavior in adult flies (Corrales-Carvajal et al., 2016), and the involvement of the mushroom bodies and the lateral horn (Wang et al., 2013; Bräcker et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Corrales-Carvajal et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2013; Bräcker et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2015

claim: Recent work has highlighted the involvement of the mushroom bodies and the lateral horn in the control of food-search behavior.
source: Although the neural circuitry that computes the cost-benefit balance remains to be identified, recent work has highlighted the crucial role played by olfaction and nutrient homeostasis in the control of food-search behavior in adult flies (Corrales-Carvajal et al., 2016), and the involvement of the mushroom bodies and the lateral horn (Wang et al., 2013; Bräcker et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2013; Bräcker et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2015
